beats.intro: Lesson twenty. [[sub]]How to choose the right mode of control, and how all three run through a working day.
beats.ideal: It is tempting to idealize cultural values. [[nice]]Everyone cares about the common good and puts it ahead of themselves. It sounds nice, even utopian. [[not]]But it is not the most efficient mode in every situation. [[tires]]It is no guide to buying tires. [[tax]]And the tax system could not run on it. [[best]]For any set of conditions there is a most appropriate mode. Our job as managers is to find it, and use it.
beats.two: Two things decide which mode fits. [[mot]]First, a person's motivation. It runs from self-interest to group interest. [[env]]Second, the environment they work in. Grove imagines a composite index of how complex, uncertain and ambiguous it is. [[cua]]He calls it the C U A factor, and it runs from low to high.
beats.cua: [[c]]A process engineer faces tricky technologies, half-working new equipment, and two groups of engineers pulling her opposite ways. Her world is complex. [[u]]A marketing manager asks to hire for his badly understaffed group. His boss waffles. He has no idea what will happen. His world is uncertain. [[a]]An Intel transportation supervisor answered to so many committees, councils and division managers that he couldn't tell which way was up. [[quit]]He finally quit. His world was ambiguous.
beats.q1: Quick check. Complex, uncertain, or ambiguous?
beats.quad: Put the two together in Grove's chart of four boxes. [[axes]]Motivation runs down the side, from self-interest at the top to group interest below. The C U A factor runs along the bottom, from low to high. [[mkt]]Self-interest, with low C U A: the market mode, like buying tires. [[con]]As motivation moves toward the group, with C U A still low: the contract, like stopping at the red light. [[cul]]Group interest and high C U A: cultural values, like helping at the accident. [[none]]And self-interest with high C U A? Nothing works. Like everyone for themselves on a sinking ship, it can only produce chaos.
beats.newhire: Apply the chart to a new employee. [[self]]A new hire is mostly self-interested, so give him a clearly structured job with a low C U A. [[well]]If he does well, he feels at home, worries less about himself, and cares more about his team. [[row]]He learns that if you are on a boat and want to get ahead, it is better to help row than to run to the front. [[promo]]Then he can be promoted into more complex, uncertain, ambiguous work, which tends to pay more. [[more]]Shared experience grows with each step. [[within]]That is why companies with strong cultures favour promotion from within. People who start in well-defined jobs learn the values, objectives and methods over time.
beats.outsider: But sometimes you must hire a senior person from outside. [[self]]Like any new hire, he arrives with high self-interest. [[trouble]]And he will almost surely be handed an organization in trouble. That is why you went outside. So his C U A is very high. [[nobase]]He has no shared experience with the rest of the company, and doesn't know its methods. [[hope]]All you can do is cross your fingers. Hope he quickly drops his self-interest and gets on top of the job, bringing the C U A down. Short of that, he is probably out of luck.
beats.day: Over a single day, we meet all three modes. [[lunch]]Take a marketing supervisor. Buying lunch in the cafeteria, he is in the market: clear choices, what he wants and what he will pay. [[come]]Coming to work at all is contractual. He is paid a set salary to do his best, and that means showing up. [[plan]]And he takes part in strategic planning, outside his regular job, because he feels the company needs what he can give. That is cultural values.
beats.project: The same holds for one project. [[train]]A training manager runs courses that teach the sales force her division's products. [[bind]]When she buys binders for the course, the market rules: the required quality, at the lowest price. [[exist]]The program itself is contractual. The salespeople expect every division to train them regularly. No written policy says so, [[bound]]but expectations can bind as firmly as a legal document. [[share]]And several divisions share one sales force. Unless each puts the common interest ahead of pushing its own products, the training becomes a free-for-all. [[coord]]Coordinating the message is cultural values at work.
beats.q4: Quick check. Which mode governs each part?
beats.monster: [[claim]]Some factory marketing managers complained that the salespeople cared only about themselves, pushing whatever earned the biggest commissions and bonuses. [[made]]But the marketing departments had created the monster. [[contest]]To win attention for their products, divisions had been running sales contests, with prizes from cash bonuses to trips to exotic places. [[time]]They were competing for a scarce and valuable resource: the salespeople's time. [[resp]]And the salespeople simply responded as you would expect.
beats.faith: But salespeople can act the other way, too. [[noprod]]Once, one of Intel's divisions ran into serious problems, and its sales engineers had nothing to sell for nearly a year. [[could]]They could have left at once, found other jobs, and earned quick commissions elsewhere. [[stay]]By and large, they stayed. They believed in the company, and had faith that things would get better. [[faith]]Belief and faith are not part of the market. They come from cultural values.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]No mode is best everywhere. Find the one that fits. [[w2]]It depends on two things: motivation, and the C U A factor. [[w3]]Self-interest with high C U A is the box where nothing works. [[w4]]Start new people in clear, low C U A jobs, and grow them from within. [[w5]]All three modes run through every day. Now the lesson practice.
beats.final1: Lesson practice. Five situations from a manager's week.
beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of lesson twenty, and of Grove's chapter on modes of control.
